{{Short description|Partial differential equation in mathematics}}
{{Distinguish|text=the [[Fisher equation]] in financial mathematics}}
<!--'Kolmogorov–Petrovsky–Piskunov equation' and 'Kolmogorov–Petrovsky–Piskounov equation' redirect here-->
[[File:FKPPwiki.jpg|thumb|Numerical simulation of the Fisher–KPP equation. In colors: the solution ''u''(''t'',''x''); in dots : slope corresponding to the theoretical velocity of the traveling wave.]]

In [[mathematics]], '''Fisher-KPP equation''' (named after [[Ronald Fisher]] {{r|digital.library.adelaide.edu.au}}, [[Andrey Kolmogorov]], [[Ivan Petrovsky]], and [[Nikolai Piskunov]]{{r|Kolmogorov-1937-SDE}}) also known as the '''Fisher equation''', '''Fisher–KPP equation''', or '''KPP equation''' is the [[partial differential equation]]:{{Equation box 1|cellpadding|border|indent=:|equation=<math> \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - D \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = r u(1-u).\, </math>|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA}}It is a kind of [[reaction–diffusion system]] that can be used to model population growth and wave propagation.

==Details==
Fisher-KPP equation belongs to the class of [[reaction–diffusion equation]]s: in fact, it is one of the simplest semilinear reaction-diffusion equations, the one which has the inhomogeneous term

:<math> f(u,x,t) = r u (1-u),\, </math>

which can exhibit traveling wave solutions that switch between equilibrium states given by <math> f(u) = 0</math>. Such equations occur, e.g., in [[ecology]], [[physiology]], [[combustion]], [[crystallization]], [[plasma physics]], and in general [[phase transition]] problems.

Fisher proposed this equation in his 1937 paper ''The wave of advance of advantageous genes'' in the context of [[population dynamics]] to describe the spatial spread of an advantageous [[allele]] and explored its travelling wave solutions.<ref name="digital.library.adelaide.edu.au">{{cite journal |first=R. A. |last=Fisher |title=The Wave of Advance of Advantageous Genes |journal=[[Annals of Eugenics]] |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=353–369 |year=1937 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-1809.1937.tb02153.x |url=https://digital.library.adelaide.edu.au/dspace/bitstream/2440/15125/1/152.pdf |hdl=2440/15125 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 
For every wave speed <math> c \geq 2 \sqrt{r D} </math> (<math> c \geq 2</math> in dimensionless form) it admits travelling [[wave]] solutions of the form

:<math> u(x,t)=v(x \pm ct)\equiv v(z),\, </math>

where <math>\textstyle v</math> is increasing and

:<math> \lim_{z\rightarrow-\infty}v\left(  z\right)  =0,\quad\lim_{z\rightarrow\infty }v\left(  z\right)  =1. </math>

That is, the solution switches from the equilibrium state ''u'' = 0 to the equilibrium state ''u'' = 1. No such solution exists for ''c''&nbsp;<&nbsp;2.<ref name="digital.library.adelaide.edu.au"/><ref name="Kolmogorov-1937-SDE">A. Kolmogorov, I. Petrovskii, and N. Piskunov. "A study of the diffusion equation with increase in the amount of substance, and its application to a biological problem." In V. M. Tikhomirov, editor, ''Selected Works of A. N. Kolmogorov I'', pages 248–270. Kluwer 1991, {{ISBN|90-277-2796-1}}. Translated by V. M. Volosov from Bull. Moscow Univ., Math. Mech. 1, 1–25, 1937</ref><ref name="Grindrod-1996-TAR">Peter Grindrod. ''The theory and applications of reaction-diffusion equations: Patterns and waves.'' Oxford Applied Mathematics and Computing Science Series. The Clarendon Press Oxford University Press, New York, second edition, 1996 {{ISBN|0-19-859676-6}}; {{ISBN|0-19-859692-8}}.</ref> The wave shape for a given wave speed is unique.  The travelling-wave solutions are stable against near-field perturbations, but not to far-field perturbations which can thicken the tail.  One can prove using the comparison principle and super-solution theory that all solutions with compact initial data converge to waves with the minimum speed.<ref>{{cite arXiv|first=Victor A. |last=Galaktionov |title=Towards the KPP-Problem and Log-Front Shift for Higher-Order Nonlinear PDEs I. Bi-Harmonic and Other Parabolic Equations |year=2012 |class=math.AP |eprint=1210.3513 }}</ref>

For the special wave speed <math>c=\pm 5/\sqrt{6}</math>, all solutions can be found in a closed form,<ref>Ablowitz, Mark J. and Zeppetella, Anthony,
''Explicit solutions of Fisher's equation for a special wave speed'', Bulletin of Mathematical Biology 41 (1979) 835–840 {{doi|10.1007/BF02462380}}</ref>  with

:<math> v(z) = \left( 1 + C \mathrm{exp}\left(\mp{z}/{\sqrt6}\right) \right)^{-2} </math>

where <math>C</math> is arbitrary, and the above limit conditions are satisfied for <math>C>0</math>.

Proof of the existence of travelling wave solutions and analysis of their properties is often done by the [[phase space method]].

==KPP equation==
In the same year (1937) as Fisher, Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov<ref name="Kolmogorov-1937-SDE" /> introduced the more general reaction-diffusion equation
:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}=F(u)</math>
where <math>F</math> is a sufficiently smooth function with the properties that
<math>F(0)=F(1)=0, F'(0)=r>0</math> and <math>F(v)>0, F'(v)<r</math> for all <math>0<v<1</math>. This too has the travelling wave solutions discussed above. Fisher's equation is obtained upon setting  <math>F(u)=ru(1-u)</math> and rescaling the <math>x</math> coordinate by a factor of <math>\sqrt{D}</math>. A more general example is given by <math>F(u)=r u(1-u^q)</math> with <math>q>0</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/pdectb/fisher2.pdf |title=Fisher-KPP Equation|last=Trefethen|date=August 30, 2001|website=Fisher 2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=Graham W. |last1=Griffiths |first2=William E. |last2=Schiesser |title=Traveling Wave Analysis of Partial Differential Equations |chapter=Fisher–Kolmogorov Equation |pages=135–146 |publisher=Academy Press |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-12-384652-5 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=G. |last=Adomian |title=Fisher–Kolmogorov equation |journal=[[Applied Mathematics Letters]] |volume=8 |issue=2 |year=1995 |pages=51–52 |doi=10.1016/0893-9659(95)00010-N |doi-access=free }}</ref>
Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov<ref name="Kolmogorov-1937-SDE" /> discussed the example with <math>q=2</math> in the context of [[population genetics]].

The minimum speed of a KPP-type traveling wave is given by

:<math>2\sqrt{\left.\frac{dF}{du}\right |_{u=0}}</math>

which differs from other type of waves, see for example [[ZFK equation|ZFK-type waves]].
